summary: A white paper on security worries about some IPng candidates, saying IPng need not improve on IPv4 but must not make security worse. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo reviews security trade-offs in candidate designs for IPng. It argues that the new protocol need not be more secure than IPv4, but should not make networks harder to defend.

questions: what security issues did rfc 1675 raise for ipng
subtitle: A review of security concerns raised by candidate IPng designs.

tldr.problem: Some candidate designs for IPng could make existing network defenses harder to use or weaken address-based security assumptions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo examines firewall filtering, packet translation, encryption and authentication, source routing, and usage accounting.
tldr.outcome: It argues that IPng need not improve on IPv4 security, but must not make security worse. It is an informational discussion, not a protocol specification.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1675 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo is a discussion of security concerns for IPng candidates.

sections.title: Security as a Design Constraint
sections.content:
Steven Bellovin submitted this memo to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550. It says that some candidate features are concerning from a security perspective and that corrective action is mandatory when a feature would otherwise harm security.

The memo considers how addressing, routing, and transition choices affect operational defenses. It does not select an IPng candidate.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo asks designers to examine the security effects of IPng choices before deployment. It does not require IPng to improve security, but says it must not make it worse.

sections.title: Firewalls, Translation, and Filtering
sections.content:
The memo says firewalls rely on hierarchical addresses and access to both source and destination addresses. Network-level firewalls may also need transport-layer fields such as TCP or UDP ports and the TCP ACK bit. Designs that make these fields harder to inspect would complicate firewall use.

For transition plans using packet translators, organizations should be able to deploy their own simple, portable, inexpensive translators. The memo warns that translators should not enable connection laundering, which could make tracing attacks harder; comprehensive logging is suggested as a possible alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls need to inspect source and destination addresses and transport fields. Transition tools should be deployable by each organization and should not make attack tracing harder.

sections.title: Encryption, Source Routing, and Accounting
sections.content:
The memo argues IPng should not hinder IP-level encryption or cryptographic authentication at host-to-host, host-to-gateway, or gateway-to-gateway levels. Tunneling can obscure the original source address, and dual-stack systems must account for all addresses assigned to a host.

Address-based authentication depends on ordinary return routing. Source routing can override that route and undermine the assumption, so the memo says cryptographic authentication should be defined and deployed before substantial use of source routing. Usage-sensitive accounting also needs reliable knowledge of address fields and a non-intrusive packet-authentication mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption should remain possible at different points in the network. If source routing changes how replies travel, systems should not rely on addresses alone to identify the sender.
